source.title: Characterizing Learning in Deep Neural Networks using Tractable Algorithmic Complexity Analysis
source.authors: Pedram Bakhtiarifard; Sophia N. Wilson; Mahmoud Afifi; Jonathan Wenshøj; Raghavendra Selvan

record.tranche_reason: Measures QuBD complexity alongside generalization-related performance and reports that they track together, using a measure distinct from those in the listed versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on algorithmic complexity and generalization-related performance. It does not test the listed versions’ specific interventions or measures. Prior-work results cited in the paper are not extracted as rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures quantized weight complexity alongside held-out performance. None of its results tests V1–V8. QuBD complexity is not magnitude-aware sharpness (V7), and the four-capacity experiment does not establish zero training error or test widening past interpolation (V2).
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors interpret learning as inducing weight structure and reducing estimated algorithmic complexity, with QuBD tracking generalization, overfitting, and grokking. They also propose its use as a compression diagnostic. These are empirical associations, not tests of V1–V8.
record.recipe_differences: Measures quantized weight complexity with QuBD and relates it to generalization-related performance; it does not reproduce the interventions or measures in the listed versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported complexity–performance relation varies with training phase: complexity increases during the described overfitting example, while its reduction continues after validation loss reaches zero in the grokking experiment.

fits_no_version.finding: Across four Fashion-MNIST MLP capacities, increasing training data improves test accuracy while lowering normalized QuBD complexity; complexity increases in the overfitting example. Tiny ViT complexity qualitatively follows its learning curves.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Normalized QuBD weight complexity tracks held-out performance in these image-classification experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: During modular-addition grokking, the normalized QuBD complexity ratio falls around delayed validation improvement and continues falling after validation loss reaches zero.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: QuBD weight complexity can track delayed generalization and continued structural simplification during grokking.

record.problems: The paper says QuBD aggregates per-bit-plane complexity assuming independence, which may overestimate underlying complexity. Some reported relationships are qualitative in the text and are presented in figures without numerical values there. The grokking result uses a modular addition task, not natural-label classification.
record.rows_left_out: No listed version was tested. Results on complexity estimation methodology, bit-plane structure, model-layer complexity, and post-training quantization were left out because they do not report outcomes on the generalization behavior named by the claim or its versions. Cited prior-work findings were also excluded.

untested.parts: Matched natural-label and fixed-random-label fitting and held-out accuracy.
Test-error changes from widening beyond the width required for zero training error, with training to convergence and no explicit regularization.
Convolutional versus fully connected test performance and the contribution of local connectivity or initialization.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer performance under specified tuning budgets and recovery recipes.
Large versus small batches under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout interventions, training-set-size dependence, excessive dropout, and removal with weight decay.
Magnitude-scaled weight-perturbation tolerance, its association with generalization gaps, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removal of examples selected by label-memorization influence versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: States are cannot_determine relative to the listed versions because all rows measure a different construct; this does not dispute their reported qualitative trends. The cited discussion of flatness and reparameterization supplies no original comparison of magnitude-aware sharpness and generalization gaps.

versions.untested_parts: Does not compare natural-label and random-label training or test accuracy.
Does not sweep network width around the interpolation threshold and report test error.
Does not compare convolutional and fully connected networks’ test error.
Does not compare adaptive optimizers with SGD on held-out performance.
Does not compare large and small batch sizes under fixed epoch budgets.
Does not test dropout’s effect on held-out error.
Does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or compare its ranking of generalization gaps.
Does not identify and remove memorized examples or measure the resulting accuracy change.

rows.subject: Four-layered MLPs (four capacities; 0.6M–13.7M trainable parameters)
rows.operation_detail: Measured normalized QuBD complexity and test accuracy as training sample count increased.

conditions.value: three random seeds; mean and standard deviation reported

rows.measure: Normalized algorithmic complexity (∆CQuBD) and test accuracy
rows.baseline: Randomly initialized counterpart for complexity; accuracy baseline not stated.
rows.value: For each model, test accuracy improves with more training data as ∆C decreases; largest model’s QuBD complexity reduces to approximately 5% of its value at initialization.
rows.uncertainty: Mean and standard deviation reported for all metrics; numerical uncertainty values not stated in the supplied text.
rows.note: Paper describes the trend across four MLPs; it does not provide individual plotted values in the text.
rows.check: The reported complexity–accuracy trend is supported, but measures no listed version. The capacity comparison uses Adam with weight decay 0.01 and reports no interpolation threshold or zero-training-error check. Section 4 varies sample counts, whereas Appendix E.3 describes 40k training samples; that reporting inconsistency should be retained.

rows.subject: MLP
rows.operation_detail: Tracked QuBD complexity alongside training and validation loss during training.
rows.value: QuBD complexity increases as the network starts to overfit.
rows.note: The text gives the direction of change, not numerical values.
rows.check: The reported increase during overfitting is supported, but QuBD complexity does not measure any listed version's effect.

rows.subject: Tiny ViT
rows.operation_detail: Tracked QuBD complexity alongside learning curves.
rows.value: ∆CQuBD tracks generalization performance and follows the learning curves.
rows.note: The text reports qualitative tracking; it provides no numerical values for this result.
rows.check: Qualitative tracking of learning curves is supported, but it does not measure any listed version's effect.

rows.subject: 2-layered MLP
rows.operation_detail: Tracked QuBD complexity during training on a modular addition task with grokking.
rows.value: Complexity reduction remains high during the high-validation-loss regime and decreases when validation loss reaches zero; it continues to decrease afterward.
rows.note: This is a grokking experiment on an algorithmic task, not same-distribution natural-label generalization.
rows.check: Replace 'complexity reduction remains high ... and decreases' with 'normalized complexity ratio remains high ... and decreases.' Equation 14 defines a trained-to-random complexity ratio; a lower ratio means greater complexity reduction. The authors' prose uses 'reduction' inconsistently. This grokking result tests no listed version.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
